title: Magic Methods
intro: **Magic methods** (or *dunder* methods, for *double underscore*) let your objects work with Python's built-in operations. `__str__` sets what `print()` shows, `__repr__` sets the developer view, `__eq__` defines `==`, `__lt__` defines `<` (and so sorting), and `__add__` defines `+`.

questions.prompt: Python calls these for you: `a + b` runs `a.__add__(b)`.
questions.explanation: Without `__eq__`, `==` only checks whether two names point to the very same object.

questions.prompt: Write `Money(amount, currency)` with `__str__` returning text like `12.50 EUR` and `__repr__` returning `Money(12.5, 'EUR')`.

tests.name: str
tests.code: assert str(Money(12.5, 'EUR')) == '12.50 EUR' and f'{Money(3, "USD")}' == '3.00 USD', 'str(Money(12.5, "EUR")) should be "12.50 EUR".'

tests.name: repr
tests.code: assert repr(Money(12.5, 'EUR')) == "Money(12.5, 'EUR')", 'repr should look like the code that creates it.'

questions.explanation: `__str__` is for users; `__repr__` is for developers and debugging.
Your object now works with a built-in function.

questions.prompt: Write `Vector(x, y)` with `__add__` (adding coordinates, returning a new Vector) and `__eq__` (same x and y).

tests.name: add
tests.code:
v = Vector(1, 2) + Vector(10, 20)
assert isinstance(v, Vector) and (v.x, v.y) == (11, 22), 'Adding vectors should add their coordinates.'

tests.name: eq
tests.code: assert Vector(3, 4) == Vector(3, 4) and not (Vector(3, 4) == Vector(4, 3)), '== should compare coordinates.'

questions.explanation: Operators are just method calls with nicer syntax.

questions.hint: It's what you see in the console and in lists.
questions.explanation: A good `__repr__` looks like the code that would create the object.

questions.prompt: `Card('A', '♠') == Card('A', '♠')` should be True but is False. Fix `__eq__`.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert Card('A', '♠') == Card('A', '♠') and not (Card('A', '♠') == Card('K', '♠')), '== should compare rank and suit.'

questions.hint: The comparison is calculated… then thrown away.
questions.explanation: Magic methods must `return` their result like any function.

questions.prompt: Fill in the method name so `sorted()` can order the parcels by weight.
Write `Playlist(songs)` supporting `len(p)`, `p[i]` (the i-th song) and `"song" in p`.

tests.name: value
tests.code:
p = Playlist(['Intro', 'Run', 'Home'])
assert len(p) == 3 and p[0] == 'Intro' and p[-1] == 'Home' and 'Run' in p and 'Gone' not in p, 'len, indexing and in should all work.'

questions.hint: `__len__`, `__getitem__` and `__contains__` each pass the work to the list.
questions.explanation: With a few dunders, your class behaves like a built-in collection.
Anywhere Python needs text for an object, it calls `__str__`.

questions.prompt: Write `Money(amount, currency)` with `__add__` (only for the same currency — otherwise raise `ValueError`), `__eq__`, `__lt__` (comparing amounts) and `__repr__` like `Money(5, 'GBP')`.

tests.name: add
tests.code: assert Money(5, 'GBP') + Money(7, 'GBP') == Money(12, 'GBP'), 'Adding the same currency should work.'

tests.name: mixed
sort
tests.code: assert sorted([Money(9, 'GBP'), Money(2, 'GBP'), Money(5, 'GBP')]) == [Money(2, 'GBP'), Money(5, 'GBP'), Money(9, 'GBP')], 'sorted should order by amount.'

questions.explanation: Operator methods should enforce the same rules as the real world.
